clue.text: These people in set, facing rogue, avenged

definitions.text: These people in set, facing rogue, avenged

parts.note: 'these people' as an object pronoun is them

indicators.note: rogue as an adjective means wayward or out of control, so these letters run wild into a new order

parts.note: once you have avenged a wrong you are 'even' with the wrongdoer

explanation.surface: A band of heroes on a film set, up against a villain, who finally get their revenge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rogue' rearranges IN SET FACING. The whole clue also describes the film's gunmen, hired to face a bandit and avenge a village.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1960 Western follows seven gunfighters hired to defend a Mexican village against a bandit, which the whole clue sketches.

clue.text: Analyst nails big time with a "male" product

indicators.note: nails here means holds fast, so the analyst wraps round the next pieces

parts.note: a tester analyses things
OS stands for outsize, a clothing size
a means one

explanation.surface: An analyst gets a huge stretch of time with a male product.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nails' means grips, so the analyst holds the next pieces; OS (outsize) is a British clothing label for large sizes.
explanation.definitionFit: This hormone, produced chiefly in the testes, drives masculine characteristics.

clue.text: "… and they all lived happily ever after"?

definitions.text: "… and they all lived happily ever after"?

parts.words: and they all lived happily ever after
parts.note: the closing line of a fairy tale, an example of a story's concluding stanza or sign-off

explanation.surface: The traditional final words of a fairy tale.
explanation.definitionFit: A closing stanza or concluding passage of a poem or book, like a story's last line.

clue.text: Having undergone changes one rang in 1954 for Queen Elizabeth the Third!

indicators.note: a bell-ringing pun: bells ring changes, and these letters undergo a change of order

explanation.surface: A bell-ringer who rang in 1954 for a coronation-era celebration.
explanation.walkthrough: Elizabeth II came to the throne in 1952, so 1954 was the third year of her reign; the Latin phrase means 'in the year of the reign'.
explanation.definitionFit: This Latin phrase dates events by a monarch's regnal year, so 1954 is her third.

clue.text: Given bar tabs, you'll craftily show

parts.note: something barred is not allowed, 'not on' in British slang

indicators.note: craftily means artfully worked, so the letters are reworked

explanation.surface: Once the bar tab is settled, you'll be shown out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not on' is British for unacceptable. The answer is a 1960s BBC comedy series with Peter Cook and Dudley Moore.
explanation.definitionFit: This was a BBC television sketch programme of the 1960s starring Peter Cook and Dudley Moore.

clue.text: Want means he left daughter destitute

indicators.note: something left destitute is reduced to ruin, so the letters are broken up and rearranged

explanation.surface: A father who walked out left his daughter penniless.
explanation.definitionFit: To lack money, to be short of means, is to suffer from being hard up, an idiom of financial hardship.

clue.text: Zero sugar, say, coating chocolate substitute

indicators.note: the sugar covers the zero, holding it inside

parts.note: sugar is an example of a carbohydrate, a carb
zero looks like the letter O

explanation.surface: A zero-sugar product is coated in chocolate.
explanation.definitionFit: Powder from the pods of this Mediterranean tree is used in place of cocoa.

clue.text: Coke tin framed by doyens off the wall

indicators.note: framed by means surrounded, so the tin sits within the rearranged letters
off the wall means crazy, so the letters go wild

parts.note: a can is a tin

explanation.surface: A tin of Coca-Cola framed and hung, then taken down by senior figures.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coke' looks like the drink, but here it is cocaine.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang for cocaine, the drug snorted up the nostrils.

clue.text: See 1
Admonishing slap here — ow! — for a change, I hypothesise

indicators.note: the exclamation spells its two letters in order, saying the first should stand in place of the second for a change

parts.note: a telling-off is a slap on the wrist, so the place for that slap is 'the wrist'

explanation.surface: Someone slapped on the wrist cries out, then muses on a hypothesis.
explanation.walkthrough: The cry 'ow' is not filler: read as O for W, it tells you to swap the W of THE WRIST for an O.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who says 'I hypothesise' is proposing ideas to explain things, which is a speculator's or thinker's job.

clue.text: Outside ground depart to catch a noon carriage

parts.note: hors is French for outside, as in hors de combat

indicators.note: to catch means to trap inside, so the rearranged letters hold the next two
ground means crushed or milled, so the letters are broken up

explanation.surface: A carriage leaving the grounds at midday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ground' turns DEPART into EDTRAP, which catches A and N.
explanation.definitionFit: A light horse-drawn vehicle, a pony and gig, is a kind of carriage.

clue.text: A very short distance to track one's initial letter

indicators.note: to track something is to follow it, so the short distance comes after the other piece
the initial of a word is its first letter, here taken from one's

parts.note: a micron is a millionth of a metre

explanation.surface: A tiny distance for tracking down the first letter of something.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the fifteenth character of the Greek alphabet, a short o.

clue.text: Direction taken from A Man with Razor, cut around snout

parts.note: starting from A you head 'to B', as in 'from A to B'

indicators.note: around means turned round, so the shortened name is read backwards
cut means docked, losing its last letter

parts.note: William of Occam is the man behind Occam's razor, the principle of choosing the simplest explanation

explanation.surface: A shaving instruction: a man with a razor trims around someone's nose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cut' drops the last letter and 'around' turns the rest backwards, giving ACCO. 'Snout' is British prison slang for tobacco.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang, especially in prisons, snout means tobacco or a cigarette.

clue.text: Strip left zilch to imagination (sniggering at the back)

indicators.note: the back of each word is its final letter, taken from each of the five words in turn

explanation.surface: A skimpy outfit leaves nothing to the imagination, and someone at the back sniggers.
explanation.definitionFit: A thong is a narrow strip of leather or cloth, as in a strap or skimpy garment.

clue.text: Annual scrambling race on fringes of course

indicators.note: the rearranged letters sit at the fringes, surrounding the other piece
scrambling means mixing up, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: 'of course' means yes, and yea is an old word for yes

explanation.surface: A yearly motorbike scramble raced around the edge of a course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'scrambling' rearranges RACE ON into ONCEAR, which surrounds YEA.
explanation.definitionFit: Something annual happens every twelve months, yearly.

clue.text: Year One singled out for concessions

parts.note: the Roman numeral for one is I

indicators.note: out here means disordered, so the letters of singled are put out of place

explanation.surface: In their first year someone was picked out for special allowances.
explanation.definitionFit: Acts of giving way are surrenders or concessions; the plural noun matches the plural definition.

clue.text: Double up refashioning citadel walls

indicators.note: walls means encloses, so the remade fortress letters wall in the other word
refashioning means remaking, so the letters are reworked

explanation.surface: Doubling up the citadel walls while rebuilding them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'refashioning' gives DLICATE from CITADEL, which walls in UP.
explanation.definitionFit: To double something is to copy it, making a replica.

clue.text: Went back up tree, say, where children play with branches

parts.note: a rec is a recreation ground, a British local park or playing field
limbed means having limbs, which for a tree are its branches

explanation.surface: A child climbs back up a tree in the playground.
explanation.walkthrough: REC is short for recreation ground, the British name for a public playing field.
explanation.definitionFit: Ascending something again, a tree being one example, is to scale it a second time.

clue.text: See 4
See 5
Animal groups lecturer and academician meet at back of pub yard

indicators.note: the two academics come at the back, after the pub and yard letters

parts.note: PH is the map abbreviation for public house
A is the abbreviation for academician, as in RA

explanation.surface: Two academics arrange to meet behind a pub's yard.
explanation.definitionFit: Phylum is the taxonomic rank just below kingdom, and these are its plural: major divisions of animals.

clue.text: Those held most dear live in a home

indicators.note: in places the verb inside the home

parts.note: a nest is a home, for birds or people
'are' means exist or live

explanation.surface: Our loved ones share our home.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition echoes the phrase 'nearest and dearest'.
explanation.definitionFit: From 'nearest and dearest', one's closest family and friends, the people one loves most.

clue.text: Blade that struggles to cut edges

indicators.note: the letters come from the edges where these words meet, the end of one and start of the next

explanation.surface: A blunt blade that struggles to cut edges.
explanation.definitionFit: This is an old type of thrusting sword, the long narrow blade of medieval swordsmen.

clue.text: Dealing with discord in ranks?

indicators.note: discord is disharmony, so the letters of the word fall out of harmony and into a new order

explanation.surface: Handling disagreement among the troops.
explanation.definitionFit: Soldiers set out in rows are lined up straight, arranged in a line.

clue.text: Poet's unworthy of town in South Wales

definitions.meaning: poetic shortening of 'beneath', as in 'beneath one', unworthy of one
a market town near Swansea in Wales

explanation.surface: A poet looks down on a Welsh town.
explanation.definitionFit: Neath is a town in Glamorgan, Wales, and the word is also a poetic form of beneath.

clue.text: Plunge nervously taken together with TV show stopper

indicators.note: acting nervously means jittering about, so these letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: Someone takes a nervous plunge into a TV show that stops everything.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the plug that closes the vent, or touch-hole, of a gun or a barrel: a type of bung.

clue.text: Equal chance of gibe (just one) from Gavin Williamson?

parts.note: A means one, as in 'a pound'
just means fair
a crack is a wisecrack or gibe
Gavin Williamson was the Conservative government's Chief Whip when this puzzle appeared

explanation.surface: A politician gives just one jibe and calls it fair.
explanation.walkthrough: The Chief Whip keeps a party's MPs in line in the UK Parliament; Gavin Williamson held that post in 2017.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means a reasonable opportunity, the same chance as everyone else.

clue.text: See 26
